headline_en: US embassy tells Bangladeshi students wishing to study in the US to apply for visas
summary_en: On 31 July 2025 the US Embassy in Dhaka posted on its official Facebook page asking qualified international students to apply quickly for student visas at approved institutions so there is enough time for visa processing. It advised students to contact the embassy's official website and relevant education service bodies for information.

facts.statement: The US Embassy in Dhaka, in a post on its official Facebook page on Thursday 31 July 2025, told qualified international students to apply quickly for their student visas for approved educational institutions so that there is enough time for visa processing, to avoid unexpected delays.
For any information, Bangladeshi students wishing to study in the US were advised (31 July 2025) to contact the US Embassy's official website and the relevant education service organisations.
Every year thousands of Bangladeshi students apply to study at various universities in the United States, according to Prothom Alo (July 2025).
Prothom Alo states that the US Embassy regularly works to simplify the visa process and supply necessary information to Bangladeshi students applying for higher study in the US.

headline_en: BSF to get 5,000 bodycams for the Bangladesh border
summary_en: India's Border Security Force (BSF) is being given about 5,000 body cameras, in two phases, for the India-Bangladesh border, to record evidence of sending back undocumented Bangladeshis and of attacks on BSF members, according to Indian security sources quoted by PTI (July 2025). Biometric equipment is also being supplied to some border posts to take fingerprints and eye scans of undocumented Bangladeshis and send them to the foreigners registration office.

facts.statement: India's Border Security Force (BSF) is being given about 5,000 body-worn video cameras, sent in two phases, for members on duty on the India-Bangladesh border, to record scenes and evidence when undocumented Bangladeshis are sent back and to monitor attacks on BSF members.

Special biometric equipment is being given to certain BSF border posts on the 4,096 km India-Bangladesh border; with it, fingerprints and eye scans of undocumented Bangladeshis will be taken and sent to the foreigners registration office (বিদেশি নিবন্ধন দপ্তর).

India's Union Home Ministry approved the two BSF headquarters proposals (bodycams and biometric devices) after a 'coordinated review' of the security situation in areas bordering Bangladesh, taken in the changed situation after the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on 5 August 2024.

The bodycams work day and night and can record about 12 to 14 hours of video continuously; they are to record incidents when BSF sends back undocumented Bangladeshis or confronts smugglers of drugs, cattle and fake Indian currency, human traffickers and infiltrators.

Bangladesh and its border force BGB have complained in various bilateral forums that the Indian side uses excessive force and unfair treatment against Bangladeshi citizens; BSF has repeatedly said it uses non-lethal or lethal weapons only as a last resort to protect soldiers' lives.

headline_en: Returnees from abroad can bring one phone a year without duty
summary_en: On 2 July 2025 Bangladesh's National Board of Revenue (NBR) amended the baggage rules so a returning passenger can bring one new mobile phone duty-free once a year, and migrants with a BMET card who stayed abroad at least six months can bring two. Duty-free gold jewellery up to 100 grams and silver jewellery up to 200 grams once a year are allowed, and a gold bar up to 10 tola once a year on duty of 5,000 taka per tola. Baggage declaration can be made online but must be submitted before leaving the customs hall.

facts.statement: Under an NBR directive issued Wednesday 2 July 2025, a passenger returning from abroad can bring one new mobile phone once a year without paying any duty (previously the baggage rules allowed one new phone on payment of duty).

Under the 2 July 2025 NBR directive, expatriates who hold a Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) card and have stayed abroad for at least six months can bring two new mobile phones a year duty-free.
Under the 2 July 2025 NBR directive, a returning passenger can bring at most 100 grams of gold jewellery once a year without duty, and 200 grams of silver jewellery.
Under the new baggage rules, a passenger can bring one gold bar of at most 10 tola weight once a year by paying duty of 5,000 taka per tola.

NBR issued the new baggage rules, the Non-Tourist Passenger Baggage Rules 2025 (অপর্যটক যাত্রী ব্যাগেজ বিধিমালা, ২০২৫), on 2 June 2025; the article says they took effect from Wednesday 2 July 2025, with amendments to make them more passenger-friendly based on views of stakeholders and field offices.

From 2 July 2025 all passengers arriving from abroad can fill in the baggage declaration form online, but submitting the baggage declaration before leaving the customs hall or area is mandatory, to prevent misuse of the facilities.

headline_en: 250 Bangladeshis register to return home from Iran
summary_en: As of 24 June 2025, 250 Bangladeshis had registered with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran to return home amid the Iran-Israel conflict; 90 of them were to be brought back overland via Pakistan (Mirjaveh to Taftan), then flown from Karachi via Dubai to Dhaka. The foreign ministry said about 2,000 Bangladeshis are in Iran, about 400 in Tehran, 672 listed with the embassy including 66 students, and gave hotline numbers.

facts.statement: As of 24 June 2025, 250 Bangladeshis had registered to return home from Iran; of them 90 were to be brought back through the Pakistan land border.
Initially women and children, along with people who had gone to Iran for medical treatment, were planned to be repatriated first, according to foreign ministry sources (June 2025).

Repatriation plan (June 2025): Bangladeshis registered with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran would be taken overland from Mirjaveh (মারজাভেহ) in Iran across the Taftan border in Pakistan's Balochistan province, then flown from Karachi with a transit in Dubai to Dhaka; other routes besides Karachi-Dubai were also being considered, and start of travel depended on the situation on the ground.

Dhaka had given Islamabad the details of about 90 Bangladeshis so they could cross from Iran into Pakistan easily; a senior government official said the top level of government had approved bringing Bangladeshis back from Iran via Pakistan.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs; senior government official

facts.statement: About 2,000 Bangladeshis were living in Iran, about 400 of them in Tehran; 672 Bangladeshis were listed (registered) in Iran, of whom 66 were students.
The foreign ministry urged all Bangladeshis in Iran wanting to return home to register quickly with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran, giving name, address and necessary information.
Hotlines for Bangladeshis in Iran (June 2025): Bangladesh Embassy, Tehran +989908577368 and +989122065745; Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Dhaka +8801712012847.

headline_en: Wife 'flees' leaving Italy expat's body at hospital
summary_en: Halim Khan (45), an Italy-based migrant from Nagargoaldi village, Rajoir, Madaripur, was found dead at Rajoir upazila health complex on 24 June 2025 after his second wife and in-laws left his body there. Relatives allege he was beaten and strangled after he returned from Italy and demanded back about 60 lakh taka he had sent his father-in-law and a motorcycle bought in his brother-in-law's name; the wife denies it and police called the death suspicious.

facts.statement: Italy-based migrant Halim Khan (45) of Nagargoaldi village, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, was allegedly called to his in-laws' house on the night of Monday 23 June 2025 and beaten and strangled to death; on the morning of 24 June his wife and mother-in-law took him to Rajoir upazila health complex and fled leaving the body after he was declared dead.

Relatives say Halim Khan, while abroad (in Italy), gave his second wife Reshma Begum's father about 60 lakh taka at various times; his brother said all of Halim's earnings from 9 years were with Reshma Begum, and money he sent to buy a motorcycle for himself before returning was used to buy one in his brother-in-law's name. After returning he demanded the money and motorcycle back, leading to quarrels.

Rajoir police OC Mohammad Masud Khan said the body was recovered from the hospital and sent to the morgue of the 250-bed Madaripur district hospital; he called the incident suspicious and said police had begun investigating. Reshma Begum denied the allegation, saying he was brought to hospital ill.
facts.source_in_article: Rajoir police OC Mohammad Masud Khan; Reshma Begum

headline_en: Bring citizens back safely (editorial)
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial (19 June 2025) urging the government to evacuate Bangladeshis from Iran during the Iran-Israel conflict. It reports the acting foreign secretary's figures (about 400 in Tehran, about 100 in contact), notes more than 2,000 Bangladeshis live in Iran including fishermen and others without papers and some in detention centres, and says air links are closed and land routes to Turkey or Pakistan are risky and costly.

facts.statement: Acting foreign secretary Ruhul Alam Siddique told a Dhaka press conference on Tuesday (17 June 2025) that about 400 Bangladeshis were in Tehran and about 100 had contacted the embassy; work had begun to move them to safety.
facts.source_in_article: Acting foreign secretary Ruhul Alam Siddique

facts.statement: More than 2,000 Bangladeshis live in Iran, some sources say more; a notable number have married Iranians and settled permanently.

Bangladeshis in Iran who live by fishing in sea areas and small jobs are the most vulnerable; many lack legal papers; some Bangladeshis are held in Iranian detention centres; some are professionals in media and health care.
In June 2025 all air links between Iran and the outside world were closed, making leaving Iran difficult; land routes to Turkey or Pakistan might be possible but are very risky and costly.

Process began to move 40 Bangladesh embassy staff in Tehran including diplomats to safe places; on Monday night ambassador Manzurul Karim Khan Chowdhury and family left the official residence. BBC Bangla reported one Bangladeshi diplomat's residence was heavily damaged in an Israeli attack.

Al Jazeera reported China, South Korea and Pakistan were already evacuating their citizens from Iran; the editorial says Bangladesh should seek help from the UN, international bodies and friendly states and should evacuate citizens whether or not they have legal papers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial citing Al Jazeera

headline_en: Canada's tightening: illegal US-Canada border crossings by Bangladeshis and Indians falling, Ottawa claims
summary_en: Canadian government documents say stricter visa policies for travellers from Mexico, India and Bangladesh cut illegal crossings from Canada into the US, and more than 2,000 Indian and Bangladeshi nationals were stopped from boarding Canada-bound flights after re-checks for visa fraud from March 2024. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) recommended about 11,050 passengers not be boarded in 2024, including 493 Bangladeshis (475 suspected of fraud). The writer, a Canada-based journalist, says many who came on visit visas with fake papers after COVID-19 crossed into the US or claimed asylum in Canada.

facts.statement: Since March 2024, re-checking of visa fraud cases led to more than 2,000 Indian and Bangladeshi nationals being prevented from boarding flights to Canada, according to a Global Affairs Canada document dated 15 January (2025).

Global Affairs Canada documents say that, owing to improved visa screening from June 2024, illegal crossings into the United States (from Canada) fell 84 percent by November 2024, and Canada's refusal rate for new visa applications reached 63 percent.

The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) said it recommended not boarding about 11,050 passengers with suspicious travel documents in 2024, including 3,250 Indian nationals (3,104 suspected of fraud) and 493 Bangladeshi nationals (475 suspected of fraud).
Canadian government documents say stricter visa policies for travellers from Mexico, India and Bangladesh reduced illegal crossings from Canada into the US.

The writer says that after COVID-19, Canada issued large numbers of visit visas to boost its economy, and lakhs of people from Bangladesh, India and elsewhere obtained Canadian visit visas using fake documents; many crossed illegally into the US and a large share claimed political asylum in Canada, with those asylum cases still pending in Canadian courts.

facts.statement: Israel struck the state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) building in Tehran with missiles on Monday 16 June 2025; three were killed and several injured, but eight Bangladeshis working in the Bangla section of Radio Tehran who were present were unharmed.

headline_en: Boat out of fuel was leaking through a cracked hull; what passengers said
summary_en: On 16 June 2025 a speedboat of Sandwip Marine Service left Guptachhara ghat, Sandwip, for Kumira despite a ban on sailing in rough weather, after pressure from passengers including some travelling abroad who would miss their flights if they could not reach Chattogram. Passengers say the boat ran out of fuel and took in water; all 27 reached shore at Akilpur, Sitakunda. The company denies running out of fuel but says it sailed under pressure from passengers going abroad; BIWTA blamed owner and driver.

facts.statement: On Monday 16 June 2025, with no boats allowed on the Sandwip-Kumira route due to bad weather, passengers including some bound abroad who would miss their flights if they could not reach Chattogram pressed a speedboat to leave Guptachhara ferry ghat, Sandwip, after 11:30 am.

Passengers said the speedboat (owned by Sandwip Marine Service) repeatedly stalled, ran out of fuel near the first buoy from the Kumira end (about 4 km / 2.8 nautical miles from Kumira ghat per a BIWTA official), and took in knee-high water through a cracked hull; all 27 passengers (including 3 children and 1 woman; one passenger said 25 to 27) reached shore at Akilpur, Sitakunda, a little before 2 pm.
facts.source_in_article: passengers Md. Alamgir, Nayan Rana, Fuad Ahmed

facts.statement: Sandwip Marine Service managing director Md. Nasir Uddin denied the boat ran out of fuel, said strong current pushed it onto shore concrete blocks cracking the hull, said the driver had been dismissed, and said the service was closed but the boat had to leave under pressure from several passengers bound abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Nasir Uddin, Sandwip Marine Service

facts.statement: BIWTA deputy director Md. Kamruzzaman blamed owner and driver, said the driver's licence would be cancelled with legal action, and said the boat left without the knowledge of BIWTA's inspector there; Sandwip UNO Rigan Chakma said the owners must take responsibility.
facts.source_in_article: BIWTA deputy director Md. Kamruzzaman; Sandwip UNO Rigan Chakma

headline_en: Bangladesh embassy in Tehran at risk; decision to move everyone quickly
summary_en: A 16 June 2025 report from the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran said the embassy is within about 1 km of Tehran University's nuclear research facility and other sensitive sites targeted by Israel, and the government decided to move all mission staff to safety, possibly moving embassy operations to a third country. About 2,000 Bangladeshis in Iran were reportedly fairly safe, most having left Tehran; 28 due to fly home on 13 June were stranded by flight suspension. The embassy set up emergency hotlines (with WhatsApp).

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy building in Tehran is within about one kilometre of at least two sensitive facilities including Tehran University's Research Institute for Nuclear Medicine (first nuclear research centre), targeted by Israeli attacks since Friday 13 June 2025, and close to one of Tehran's two main IT centres; the mission reported diplomats' and staff families needed to move 30-40 km outside the city.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Embassy Tehran report to foreign ministry, 16 June 2025

facts.statement: After the report, an immediate decision was made to move everyone at the mission including diplomats to safe places; officials said finding suitable safe housing outside Tehran was difficult and moving the embassy's work to a third country was being considered if needed.
About 2,000 Bangladeshis in Iran were reported fairly safe as of 16 June 2025, almost all of them having moved outside Tehran; an official said Israel had announced Tehran should be evacuated.
28 Bangladeshis who were due to return home on 13 June 2025 were stranded in Iran because flights stopped; the foreign ministry learned that more than a hundred Bangladeshis in all were in Tehran.

Bangladeshis in Tehran include about 40 at the embassy (ambassador, two officers, five staff and families), 27 linked to the eight Bangladeshis at Radio Tehran with families, about 10 to 12 students and about 10 professionals.

About 600 Bangladeshis in several places in Iran have lived there over 30 years and settled through marriage; about 800 more have stayed illegally for over 10 years working in various sectors; about 200 students study in Iran; and 300 to 500 Bangladeshis are always in Iran as a human-trafficking transit country waiting to be trafficked onward.
In a special notice on Sunday 15 June 2025 the Bangladesh Embassy in Iran set up an emergency hotline for Bangladeshis living in Iran: +989908577368 and +989122065745 (including WhatsApp).

headline_en: Returnee Shah Alam, successful at chui jhal farming, says 'I won't go abroad again'
summary_en: Shah Alam (45) of Niamatpur village, Sirajganj Sadar, returned after about 12 years in Saudi Arabia and in 2022 began commercial chui jhal (a spice vine) farming with help from local NGO National Development Programme (NDP) under a PKSF high-value spice demonstration. He says he spent 1.17 lakh taka and sold 7.37 lakh taka worth this year, and urges young people to farm at home instead of going abroad.

facts.statement: Returnee Shah Alam (45), son of Shukur Ali of Niamatpur village, Shialkol union, Sirajganj Sadar, spent about 12 years in Saudi Arabia, then on 30 August 2022 leased 33 decimals of land beside his home for 3 years for 60,000 taka to start chui jhal cultivation.

Shah Alam started with support from local NGO National Development Programme (NDP), which implements high-value spice crop demonstrations under the integrated agriculture unit of Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF).

Shah Alam says he has spent 1,17,000 taka on chui jhal since starting and this year (2025) sold 7,37,000 taka worth in two phases; wholesalers from Khulna and elsewhere buy from his field. He plans two more bighas of chui jhal and has started papaya on three bighas.

Per the district Department of Agricultural Extension, raw chui jhal sells for 700 to 1,500 taka per kg and dried for 1,500 to 3,000 taka; one hectare of bush chui jhal can yield about 2 to 2.5 metric tons a year.
Shah Alam, addressing unemployed youth, said he will not go abroad again and wants to farm at home, and that farmers and young people could profit from chui jhal, which has demand at home and abroad.

headline_en: Unconscious husband finally brought back from abroad; wife in another fight to make him well
summary_en: Abdul Jabbar Sardar (45) of Hiranandapur, Tanore, Rajshahi went to Saudi Arabia on 16 January 2018 after borrowing 7 lakh taka; brokers 'sold' him as an airport cleaner who worked three years unpaid and was then turned out with nothing. Undocumented, he later worked at an Indian-owned tile factory, was badly injured in a road accident on 10 May 2024 and spent a year in ICU; his wife's appeals to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board failed, but the Tanore UNO reached the embassy and he was flown home unconscious in May 2025 and admitted to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital ICU.

facts.statement: Abdul Jabbar Sardar went to Saudi Arabia as a worker on 16 January 2018; on landing he was put to work as a cleaner and later realised brokers had 'sold' him as an airport 'cleaner'; for three years he worked cleaning at the airport without pay and was then sent away from the airport empty-handed.
Abdul Jabbar Sardar raised 7 lakh taka by borrowing to go to Saudi Arabia in 2018; the loan had still not been repaid as of May 2025.
Thinking Saudi police would send him home if caught, Jabbar surrendered to police himself; police took his fingerprints and released him again, and he was left with no money for food.
A man from Mondumala, Tanore, Rajshahi named Moazzem, whom Jabbar met by chance, got him a job at a tile factory owned by an Indian national, where he worked without papers.
On 10 May 2024 Jabbar was seriously injured in a road accident in Saudi Arabia; Saudi law enforcement took him to a local hospital and he was in ICU for about a year.

About three months after the accident, the people Adori Khatun dealt with (via the Indian employer) asked for 70 lakh taka to send Jabbar home because he had no papers; later they asked her to pay 19,000 taka for the air fare, which she could not raise.
On the Indian company owner's advice, Adori Khatun applied through the Wage Earners' Welfare Board in Dhaka for her husband's return, but it did not work.

Adori Khatun waited 22 days at the Tanore Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) office without being let in; after she cried out, a police member took her inside; the UNO tried to contact the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, got through after 15 days, and connected her to them by phone.

On 13 May 2025 Adori was called and told to keep a bed ready at the hospital where the patient would be admitted in Dhaka, and was told a doctor and nurse would accompany him and hand him over at the hospital and that some money would be given; on arrival in Dhaka they gave no money, did not go to the hospital and left the patient at the airport.

After return, seven hours at a private hospital in Dhaka cost 70,000 taka; Adori then hired a vehicle with oxygen for 25,000 taka and on Saturday (24 May 2025) brought him to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital, where an ICU bed was available only from Sunday (article gives both 25 May and 26 May).

Rajshahi Medical College Hospital ICU in-charge Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal said Jabbar had become skeletal after a year in ICU abroad, needs much nutrition and a head operation, after which he might regain consciousness; his son was being trained to feed him before moving him to the general ward.
facts.source_in_article: Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal, ICU in-charge, RMCH

facts.statement: Adori Khatun says the family is indebted, has no means even to eat, let alone pay for treatment, and lives on loans.

headline_en: Three exams for Bangladeshi doctors and nurses to build careers in Ireland
summary_en: A contributor in Ireland explains that Ireland's health system relies heavily on foreign doctors and nurses, but Bangladeshis are few because the Irish Medical Council (IMC) and nursing board (NMBI) do not readily recognise Bangladeshi degrees, there is no government supply agreement, sponsorship is hard to get, and IELTS 7.0 or OET B is required. Doctors generally go through IMC registration, the PRES exam if the degree is unrecognised, or an alternative via PLAB or MRCP. Salaries are given, and he recommends government action.

facts.statement: As of 2023 about 40 percent of all doctors working in Ireland were foreign, and about 51.8 percent of Ireland's nursing workforce were trained abroad.

The Irish Medical Council (IMC) readily recognises medical degrees from India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Egypt, but recognition is hard for Bangladeshi degrees, so Bangladeshi doctors face extra exams that are time-consuming and costly.

Ireland's nursing board (NMBI) recognises nurses from the Philippines, India and Nigeria because of formal agreements; with no such agreement with Bangladesh, Bangladeshi nurses face various complications when applying.

Bangladeshi doctors usually go through three main steps to work in Ireland: (1) registration with the Irish Medical Council (IMC), depending on experience and qualifications; (2) the PRES (Pre-Registration Examination System) exam if the degree is not recognised, which includes a written exam, a clinical skills exam and a supervised internship; (3) an alternative route: doctors who have passed PLAB or MRCP can get IMC registration without PRES.

To work as a specialist in Ireland a doctor needs CESR (Certificate of Eligibility for Specialist Registration) or equivalent; even after passing PRES, a language test (IELTS or OET) is mandatory for IMC registration.
Doctors and nurses working in Ireland must score at least 7.0 in IELTS or grade 'B' in OET.

Applying directly to Irish hospitals requires sponsorship, which is hard for Bangladeshis to get; India and some other countries have dedicated recruitment agencies linking with hospitals, but there is nothing similar for Bangladeshis.
Ireland has formal health-worker supply agreements with the Philippines, India, Nigeria and Sudan; Bangladesh has no such agreement.

Thousands of health workers from India, Pakistan, Philippines, Egypt, Sudan and Nigeria work in Ireland, but Bangladeshi doctors are very few and Bangladeshi nurses almost none; most Bangladeshi doctors working in Ireland came from various Middle Eastern countries.
Ireland runs a 'Critical Skills Employment Permit' programme through which certain professionals get work permission easily; the writer suggests Bangladesh seek inclusion for doctors and nurses.
Demand in Ireland is high for specialist doctors, especially in anaesthesia, cardiology, neurology and surgery.

In Ireland an entry-level doctor can earn about 50,000 to 60,000 euros a year, specialists 120,000 to 200,000 euros, and consultants more than 210,000 euros; nurses start at about 30,000 euros a year at entry level and can exceed 55,000 euros at senior level.

The writer recommends Bangladesh negotiate recognition with IMC and NMBI, sign a formal health-worker supply agreement with Ireland, set up government IELTS/OET training and English-medium teaching in medical and nursing colleges, and create reliable recruitment agencies linking with Irish hospitals.

headline_en: A piece of Bangladesh in the desert, organised by cricket lovers
summary_en: A press-release style piece on the Bangladesh Cricket Association Kuwait, a volunteer-run expatriate sports body started about six years earlier, which holds tournaments for Bangladeshi workers in Kuwait. It held its Independence Cup 2025 prize-giving and cultural evening on 16 May 2025 at a resort in Hijil, Kuwait, attended by Bangladesh embassy officials.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Cricket Association Kuwait, started about six years before 2025 by a few expatriate cricket lovers, organises regular cricket tournaments for Bangladeshi migrants in Kuwait (Independence Cup, Victory Day Cup, Hala February Cup), with unpaid volunteers who play on Fridays and holidays; it aims to help young migrants overcome loneliness and depression and plans a Bangladeshi sports academy in Kuwait.

On Friday 16 May 2025 the association held the Independence Cup Cricket Tournament 2025 prize-giving and cultural evening at a resort in the desert area of Hijil, Kuwait; Keraniganj Challengers won and Jeleeb Probashi were runners-up.

Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait officials named at the event: Minister (Labour) Mohammad Abul Hossain; Counsellor and Head of Chancery Mohammad Moniruzzaman; Ambassador Major General Syed Tareq Hossain (was to be chief guest but was in hospital).

headline_en: ILO country director advises more investment in employment-oriented education
summary_en: At a press conference in Dhaka on 19 May 2025 before leaving, ILO Bangladesh country director Tuomo Poutiainen said many Bangladeshi workers going abroad lack job security, the sending process lacks transparency and too much money is taken from them, and building a skilled workforce would make outgoing workers more aware. He also urged investment in technical education, social protection and labour law reform.

facts.statement: ILO country director in Bangladesh Tuomo Poutiainen said on 19 May 2025 that workers going abroad from Bangladesh often have no guarantee of work, there is lack of transparency in sending them abroad, and far too much money is taken from them.

Poutiainen said that if a skilled workforce can be built, people going abroad will be more aware of these issues (job guarantees, opaque process, excess costs); he urged government attention to investment in technical education.

Poutiainen, ILO country director in Bangladesh since 4 June 2018, was to leave on 31 May 2025 to become ILO's deputy regional director for Asia and the Pacific; he recommended implementing the Labour Reform Commission's proposals and amending the labour law in workers' interests.

Former minister Imran moved from jail to hospital with various ailments
summary_en: Former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad, arrested on 20 October 2024 and remanded in a case under the human trafficking prevention law, was moved from Sylhet Central Jail to Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital on 13 May 2025 with diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

facts.statement: Former five-time MP for Sylhet-4 Imran Ahmad, who became state minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in 2018 and full minister of that ministry the next year, was arrested by Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Police from Banani, Dhaka, on the night of 20 October 2024; the next day he was taken on remand in a case filed at Paltan police station under the human trafficking prevention law, and was later shown arrested in several cases in Dhaka and Sylhet.

On Tuesday 13 May 2025 Imran Ahmad was taken from Sylhet Central Jail to Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, where he was in cabin 13, ward 10, under observation for diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

headline_en: Why learn Chinese, where to learn it, what opportunities
summary_en: Md. Kamruzzaman, studying civil engineering at China Three Gorges University on a Chinese government scholarship after learning Chinese at Dhaka University's Confucius Institute, describes why and where to learn Chinese in Bangladesh. Confucius Institutes or classrooms run at Dhaka University, North South University and Shanto-Mariam University; Chinese firms in Bangladesh hire interpreters at 30,000-50,000 taka a month without experience; learning takes about one to two years.

facts.statement: Confucius Institutes or 'Confucius Classrooms' operate at Dhaka University, North South University and Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology, with one being set up at Rajshahi University; limited Chinese courses run at BRAC University, Chittagong University, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Jahangirnagar University and Daffodil International University; Dhaka University offers a bachelor's degree in Chinese. Chinese teachers at Confucius Institutes teach directly in English.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: Some Bangladeshis who studied in China have set up private training centres offering 6-month to 1-year online and offline Chinese courses.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: The writer studies civil engineering at China Three Gorges University on a Chinese government scholarship after learning Chinese at Dhaka University's Confucius Institute; he says Chinese government scholarships are available and Chinese is also valued in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries.

facts.statement: In Chinese companies in Bangladesh one can work as an interpreter without experience at usually 30,000 to 50,000 taka a month, rising to 1 to 2 lakh taka with experience, with possible promotion to management.

facts.statement: Chinese is among the hardest languages; mastering it usually takes one to two years (one year with hard work), and the risk of dropping out rises after starting level 3.

headline_en: Will the government walk the old path on Rangpur's deprivation? (column)
summary_en: Column (4 May 2025) by Tuhin Wadud arguing Rangpur division is neglected in development. He says he doubts Rangpur division accounts for even 1 percent of Bangladeshis working abroad, and suggests the government give special training and easy-term loans to send workers from Rangpur abroad.

facts.statement: The columnist doubts whether the whole of Rangpur division accounts for even 1 percent of Bangladesh's migrant workers abroad, and says it seems some single upazilas elsewhere have more people abroad than all of Rangpur division (his impression, no source given).
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Wadud, professor, Begum Rokeya University (column)

facts.statement: The columnist suggests the interim government give special training and loans on easy terms to people in Rangpur division who could be sent abroad for work, and start sending them.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Wadud, professor, Begum Rokeya University (column)
